before: Our age is putting on ein wirklicher Ausverkauf — a genuine clearance sale — and not only in trade: in the realm of ideas too. Everything can be had at such a rock-bottom price that one begins to wonder whether in the end anyone will still want to bid. Every speculative billiard-marker who conscientiously keeps score of the momentous progress of modern philosophy, every private lecturer, tutor and student, every smallholder and lodger in philosophy, does not stop at doubting everything but goes further. It would perhaps be untimely and inopportune to ask them where they actually get to. But it is surely polite and modest to take it as settled that they have doubted everything; otherwise it would be a strange thing to say, that they went further. This preliminary movement, then, they have all made — and presumably so easily that they do not find it necessary to let fall a single word about how. For not even the person who anxiously and with concern looked for a little enlightenment found any: not a guiding hint, not a small dietary prescription for how one is to conduct oneself under this enormous task. “But surely Descartes did it?” Descartes, a venerable, humble and upright thinker whose writings no one, surely, can read without the deepest emotion, did as he said and said as he did. Alas! Alas! Alas! In our time that is a great rarity! Descartes, as he himself repeats often enough, did not doubt with regard to faith. (“Memores tamen, ut jam dictum est, huic lumini naturali tamdiu tantum esse credendum, quamdiu nihil contrarium a Deo ipso revelatur ..... Præter cætera autem, memoriæ nostræ pro summa regula est infigendum, ea quæ nobis a Deo revelata sunt, ut omnium certissima esse credenda; et quamvis forte lumen rationis, quam maxime clarum et evidens, aliud quid nobis suggerere videretur, soli tamen auctoritati divinæ potius quam proprio nostro judicio fidem esse adhibendam.” [Remembering, however, as has already been said, that this natural light is to be trusted only so long as nothing to the contrary is revealed by God himself ..... Above all, though, we must fix in our memory as the supreme rule that what God has revealed to us is to be believed as the most certain of all things; and even if perhaps the light of reason, however clear and evident, should seem to suggest something else to us, we must still put our faith in divine authority alone rather than in our own judgment.] Cf. Principia philosophiæ, part one, § 28 and § 76.) He did not cry “Fire!” and make it everyone’s duty to doubt; for Descartes was a quiet, solitary thinker, not a bellowing night watchman in the street. He modestly admitted that his method had significance only for himself, and that it arose in part from the muddle his earlier learning had been in. (“Ne quis igitur putet, me hic traditurum aliquam methodum, quam unusquisque sequi debeat ad recte regendam rationem; illam enim tantum, quam ipsemet secutus sum, exponere decrevi... Sed simul ac illud studiorum curriculum absolvi (sc. juventutis, quo decurso mos est in eruditorum numerum cooptari, plane aliud coepi cogitare. Tot enim me dubiis totque erroribus implicatum esse animadverti, ut omnes discendi conatus nihil aliud mihi profuisse judicarem, quam quod ignorantiam meam magis magisque detexissem.” [So let no one suppose that I mean to hand down here some method that everyone ought to follow in order to guide his reason rightly; for I have resolved to set out only the one I myself have followed... But as soon as I had finished that course of study (namely, of my youth), at the end of which it is the custom to be admitted to the ranks of the learned, I began to think something quite different. For I found myself entangled in so many doubts and so many errors that I judged that all my efforts to learn had done me no other good than to uncover my ignorance more and more.] Cf. Dissertatio de methodo, pp. 2 and 3.) — The ancient Greeks, who did after all know something about philosophy too, held doubting to be the task of a whole life, because the skill of doubting is not acquired in days or weeks. The old veteran among them, who had served his full time, attained it: through every snare he had held doubt in equilibrium, had fearlessly denied the certainty of the senses and the certainty of thought, and had incorruptibly withstood the anxiety of self-love and the insinuations of fellow-feeling. What the Greeks took for a life’s task and their veteran attained — that is what everyone in our time begins with.

before: It was early morning. Abraham rose early, had the donkeys saddled and left his tent, taking Isaac with him; but from the window Sarah followed them with her eyes, down through the valley, until she could no longer see them. For three days they rode in silence. On the morning of the fourth day Abraham said not a single word, but raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah far off. He left the young servants behind and, with Isaac by the hand, went up the mountain alone. But Abraham said to himself: “At any rate I will not hide from Isaac where this road is leading him.” He stopped and laid his hand on Isaac’s head to bless him, and Isaac bent down to receive the blessing. And Abraham’s face was fatherliness itself, his look gentle, his speech full of exhortation. But Isaac could not understand him; his soul could not be lifted up. He threw his arms around Abraham’s knees, he fell pleading at his feet, he begged for his young life, for his bright hopes; he reminded him of the joy in Abraham’s house, he reminded him of the sorrow and the loneliness. Then Abraham raised the boy up and led him along by the hand, speaking words of comfort and exhortation. But Isaac could not understand him. Abraham climbed Mount Moriah, but Isaac did not understand him. Then for a moment Abraham turned away from him; but when Isaac looked at Abraham’s face a second time, it had changed. His look was wild, his figure was horror. He gripped Isaac by the chest, flung him to the ground and said: “Stupid boy, do you believe I am your father? I am an idol-worshipper. Do you believe it is God’s command? No, it is my own desire.” Then Isaac trembled and in his anxiety cried out: “God in heaven, have mercy on me! God of Abraham, have mercy on me! If I have no father on earth, be my father yourself!” But Abraham whispered to himself: “Lord in heaven, I thank you. After all, it is better that he believes I am a monster than that he loses his faith in you.”

before: It was early morning. Abraham rose early and embraced Sarah, the bride of his old age, and she kissed Isaac, her pride, her hope through all generations, who had taken away her shame. Then they rode in silence along the road, and Abraham’s eyes were fixed on the ground until the fourth day, when he raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah a long way off, but his eyes turned again to the ground. Without a word he arranged the wood and bound Isaac; without a word he drew the knife. Then he caught sight of the ram that God had chosen. That he sacrificed, and went home. — — — From that day on, Abraham aged; he could not forget that God had demanded it of him. Isaac flourished as before; but Abraham’s eye was darkened, and he saw joy no more.

IV

It was early morning. In Abraham’s house everything had been made ready for the journey. He took his leave of Sarah; the faithful servant Eliezer went with him a stretch of the way and then turned back. Abraham and Isaac rode on together in harmony until they reached Mount Moriah. But Abraham prepared everything for the sacrifice, calm and gentle; yet as he turned away and drew the knife, Isaac saw Abraham’s left hand clench in despair and a trembling pass through his body — but Abraham drew the knife.

before: Now and then one can hear people complain, when some eccentric head stirs up a whirlwind of doubt; then they say: “If only he had kept silent!” Faust makes this idea real. Whoever has a notion of what it means for a human being to live on spirit also knows what doubt’s hunger is, and that the doubter is as hungry for life’s daily bread as for the nourishment of spirit. Now, all the pain Faust suffers may be a pretty good argument that it is not pride that has possessed him. Even so, I will use a little precaution, which I can easily invent. For just as Gregory of Rimini was called tortor infantium — torturer of infants — because he held that little children are damned, so I could be tempted to call myself tortor heroum — torturer of heroes; for I am most inventive where torturing heroes is concerned. Faust sees Margaret — not after he has chosen pleasure, for my Faust does not choose pleasure at all. He does not see Margaret in Mephistopheles’s concave mirror; he sees her in all her lovable innocence. And since his soul has kept its love for people, he is also quite capable of falling in love with her. But he is a doubter; his doubt has annihilated actuality for him. For my Faust is so ideal that he does not belong among those scholarly doubters who doubt for one hour each semester from the lectern but otherwise can do everything else — just as they do the doubting too — without being in a state of spirit or acting by virtue of spirit. He is a doubter, and the doubter is as hungry for joy’s daily bread as for the food of spirit. Still, he stays true to his resolve and keeps silent: he speaks to no one about his doubt, and to Margaret not about his love either.

before: But now Abraham — how did he act? For I have not forgotten, and the reader may now perhaps be good enough to remember, that it was in order to run up against this point that I entered into the whole preceding investigation. It was not so that Abraham would thereby become more understandable, but so that his incomprehensibility might become more disjointed. For, as I have said, Abraham I cannot understand; him I can only admire. It was also remarked that none of the stages described contained an analogy to Abraham. They were developed only so that, shown within their own sphere, each might, at the moment it deviated like a compass needle, point as it were to the boundary of the unknown land. Insofar as there could be any question of an analogy, it would have to be the paradox of sin. But that in turn lies in another sphere; it cannot explain Abraham, and is itself far easier to explain than Abraham.
